name: protected-system
intent: Give a resource exactly one owning object whose published operations are the only way to touch it, so that every access is decided by an authorization check before the resource is used.
problem: A resource - a credential store, a file tree, a socket, a connection pool, a device handle - is referenced from many places. When each use site performs its own permission check, the checks drift, new code paths forget them, and the resource remains reachable as a raw handle, so a missing check cannot even be detected. The recurring trigger: one object can own the resource and clients can be made to hold only that object, so ownership itself can carry the enforcement.
context: Applies where ownership is expressible in the language or runtime (private field, unexported type, opaque handle, module boundary) and an authorization policy - identity, role, permission, capability - can be evaluated at each public operation. The guard may sit in-process (object or module scope) or at a process/kernel boundary, where the same pattern becomes a real reference monitor; the assurance the implementation can claim depends on which side of that line it lives.
benefits: The set of ways into the resource becomes enumerable: one object owns it, so new callers cannot invent an access path the design did not foresee, and review has a single place to look at.
The decision and the operation are one call: the guard checks immediately before it performs the operation, so no check-then-use window exists for the caller to exploit.
Policy changes and revocation take effect at the next call, because no caller ever holds the resource itself.
Denials become uniform and observable: the guard refuses (or throws) from one place, where denials can be logged, metered and alarmed on.
The resource's implementation can change behind the guard's interface - storage, caching, remote access - without touching callers, as long as the guard's policy obligations stay intact.
Testability of the enforcement itself: grant, deny and error behaviour can be exercised against the guard without the resource participating in the security decision.
tradeoffs: The guarantee is exactly as strong as the encapsulation: reflection (setAccessible, getattr, send, MethodHandles), unsafe code, serialization, a debugger, or a framework that is handed the raw resource defeats the ownership the pattern relies on - in-process guards therefore document discipline, not a security boundary, unless the runtime enforces invisibility (module system, opaque handle, separate process).

One object now mediates every operation: its public surface grows with each use case, it becomes the contention point for concurrent access, and it degenerates into a god object unless the policy stays in a separate source and the surface is kept deliberately narrow.

A guard inside the same trust domain cannot defend against code that already has equal privileges; the reference-monitor properties (non-bypassable, always invoked, tamper-proof, evaluable) require placing the enforcement below the application, in a kernel, hypervisor or separate process.

Per-access policy evaluation plus an extra forwarding hop costs latency and throughput; caching decisions to recover it re-opens the revocation hole unless the cache is invalidated when authority changes.

Correct delegation is subtle: returning the raw resource - a reference, a descriptor, a mutable copy, an iterator that exposes internals - re-opens every path the pattern closed, so the guard must return guarded views, copies or revocable capabilities and must own their lifetime.

Failure handling must be designed in: if the policy source is unreachable or the caller carries no identity, the guard must deny (fail-safe default); a guard that treats an unanswerable check as permission is bypassed by its own error path.

participants.responsibility: Calls the guard's published operations and holds no reference to the resource itself; it may carry the identity the policy is evaluated against.

participants.role: Protection Guard (Protection Proxy / Protected System object)
participants.responsibility: Owns the resource, evaluates the policy on every published operation, forwards permitted operations and denies the rest - the decision and the access happen in the same call.
The object being protected (data, handle, connection, device, subsystem); it is reachable only through the guard and never handed out in raw form.
Where the rule lives - permissions, roles, ACLs, capabilities or tokens; the guard asks it per access so that revocations and rule changes take effect immediately.

participants.role: Trusted Owner (Factory / Composition Root / Module Boundary)
participants.responsibility: The only code allowed to construct the resource and the guard; it wires the policy in and hands clients the guard, never the resource.

use_cases: Credential and key stores: an in-process vault owns the keys and exposes only operations (sign, decrypt, rotate), so callers never receive the secret material.
Storage gateways: a library owns the directory handle or object-store client and applies path and tenant rules on every operation instead of handing out a raw client.
Pools: the pool owns its connections and leases checked-out views, so a caller cannot keep, share or resurrect a connection the pool must reclaim.
Multi-tenant data access: a tenant-scoped repository wrapper pins the tenant filter and refuses operations that would query outside it.
Device and driver access: a supervisor object owns the device handle and validates commands, or a privileged daemon owns the socket and checks each request from an unprivileged client.
Module-level boundaries: a package exports only the guard type and keeps the resource unexported, so code outside the package cannot even name the protected representation.
Linux Landlock: a kernel-enforced ruleset restricts a process and its future children to explicitly allowed filesystem or network rights, placing mediation below application code.
Kubernetes RBAC: the API server evaluates Roles and bindings for each API request, mediating verbs and resources instead of exposing the cluster's backing store to clients.
HashiCorp Vault policies: authenticated tokens are checked against path and capability rules before secret operations, while the storage backend remains behind the Vault service.
avoid_when: The platform already mediates the resource (kernel syscalls and file permissions, database row security, container sandbox, managed-service identity): configure that mechanism instead of rebuilding it in application code.
The resource is reached from one tight private scope that never escapes: a local variable plus a helper function is simpler than a guard object.

Callers legitimately need raw, high-throughput access (a hot inner loop, a large buffer, a batch import): check at the boundary and transfer ownership explicitly, rather than paying a proxy call per element.

The resource cannot actually be made unreachable (the framework, DI container or another component hands out the raw reference): the guard would be advisory - fix ownership first or accept that the boundary has to be process-level.

The requirement is that every path is mediated, including admin, batch, recovery and internal callers: that is complete-mediation/reference-monitor territory, a system-wide property that one owning object cannot prove on its own.
anti_patterns: Facade without ownership: a checked wrapper exists, but the raw resource is still public elsewhere, so a second path skips the check.
Leaky guard: the guard checks permissions and then hands back the underlying handle, reference or mutable copy, after which the caller is unchecked.
Documented security: relying on private/internal/underscore conventions as a boundary while reflection, unsafe code or foreign-function access can reach the resource.
God guard: every new use case adds a method with inline policy logic until the object owns both the resource and the whole business model.
Fail-open guard: a policy lookup error, missing identity or timeout is treated as permission.
design_principles: Least privilege: a caller receives the narrowest interface its task needs, never the resource itself.
Information hiding: the existence, location and representation of the resource are private to the guard.
Separation of concerns: policy (what is allowed), enforcement (that it is applied) and resource behaviour are three separate things.
Fail-safe defaults: if the guard cannot decide, the answer is deny.
Defence in depth: an in-process guard is one layer; the platform (process, kernel, container) is the layer that survives a compromised runtime.
best_practices: Make the resource unreachable: private field, unexported type, opaque handle, module boundary - and no getter, cast or friend that widens it again.
Decide inside the operation: resolve identity and policy in the same method that touches the resource, and deny when either is unavailable.
Keep policy in a separate, replaceable source; the guard asks and enforces, it does not invent rules.
Design the public surface deliberately: one operation per use case, narrow signatures, never a passthrough of the resource type.
Return guarded views, copies or revocable capabilities - never the raw resource - and define what happens to operations already in flight when access is revoked.
Log and meter denials from the guard, and treat as a defect any path (reflection, serialization, DI wiring, debugger, admin tooling) that can obtain the raw resource.
Pair the in-process guard with process/kernel-level mediation where the threat model includes code that runs with the same privileges.
sources: Schumacher, Fernandez-Buglioni, Hybertson, Buschmann & Sommerlad, Security Patterns: Integrating Security and Systems Engineering, Wiley 2006 (the catalog's source line dates it 2005) - the security-patterns catalog this row belongs to; see docs/design-patterns.md (Sources, §8 Enforcement points).

Gamma, Helm, Johnson & Vlissides, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software, Addison-Wesley 1994 - the Proxy pattern's protection-proxy variant: 'A protection proxy controls access to the original object. Protection proxies are useful when objects should have different access rights.'

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Security_pattern - the protected system pattern 'provides some reference monitor or enclave that owns the resources and therefore must be bypassed to get access. The monitor enforces as the single point a policy. Design Patterns refers to it as "Protection Proxy".'
